claims.text: The onset and progression of phase transition in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is primarily governed by size-dependent surface disordering.
Smaller FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles develop premelted surface layers at lower temperatures than larger particles.
Enhanced atomic mobility and nanoscale melting-point depression cause the earlier surface premelting of smaller particles.
Premelted surface layers nucleate complete melting.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are fully crystalline and solid, with controlled size distributions.
Particles smaller than 10 nm and larger than 30 nm will be compared under an identical 10 K/min heating ramp in argon.
The premelted disordered layer originates at nanoparticle edges.
The premelted disordered layer acts as the nucleation site for full melting.
Smaller nanoparticles have a lower energy barrier for surface-atom mobility.
Surface premelting propagates inward and triggers complete melting.
Smaller particles melt at a lower temperature than larger particles.
Surface disordering will be observable through changes in TEM image contrast or diffraction patterns.
DSC will show a lower melting temperature for smaller nanoparticles than for larger nanoparticles.
Atomistic simulations will show significantly lower barriers to surface disordering in smaller particles.
Oxidative atmospheres or non-standard heating rates may alter the observed transition behavior.
The exact transition temperatures and magnitude of melting-point depression may vary with particle-size distribution and experimental details.
Molecular-dynamics simulations can identify atomistic rearrangement or nucleation mechanisms in high-temperature nanoparticle and high-entropy-alloy studies.
